items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a testable statement that predicts the relationship between two variables”?
items.answer: Hypothesis
items.markingKey: Hypothesis: a testable statement that predicts the relationship between two variables. [1]

items.stem: Explain why controlled variables are important in an investigation.
items.answer: If other variables change, they could affect the dependent variable, so any pattern could not be attributed to the independent variable; controlling them makes the test fair and results valid.
items.markingKey: other factors affect results [1]; makes conclusions valid [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain the purpose of a pilot study.
items.answer: To test equipment, methods and questionnaires on a small scale, identify problems, estimate time needed and decide sample size, so the main study is more reliable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [3]

items.stem: A group is investigating whether trampling on a footpath affects plant species diversity in a park near Cairo. State two variables that should be controlled.
items.answer: Quadrat size, time of year, soil type, slope.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Chloe is investigating whether light intensity affects the height of plants growing under a woodland canopy. (a) Write a null hypothesis. (b) State two variables that should be controlled.
items.answer: (a) There is no relationship between light intensity and plant height. (b) Plant species, soil type, time of day light is measured, slope.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A class investigates whether the number of people using a beach affects the amount of litter found on beaches near Lisbon. The class has one day for data collection. The hypothesis is: “There is more litter on beaches with more visitors.” (a) Explain two limitations of a one-day study. (b) Explain how the reliability of the results could be improved.
items.answer: (a) Conditions on one day may not be typical (weather, season); limited sample size; no repeats on other days; time constraints may lead to rushed measurements. (b) Increase the number of samples; repeat on different days or seasons; use calibrated equipment; take means of repeats.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per limitation with explanation up to [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Explain why risk assessment is part of planning fieldwork.
items.answer: Fieldwork may involve hazards such as rivers, traffic, weather or chemicals; identifying risks and precautions keeps investigators safe.

items.stem: A researcher is investigating whether noise from traffic affects the number of bird species heard in urban parks in Riyadh. The researcher has one day for data collection. The hypothesis is: “Fewer bird species are recorded where traffic noise is higher.” (a) Explain two limitations of a one-day study. (b) Explain how the reliability of the results could be improved.
items.answer: (a) Conditions on one day may not be typical (weather, season); limited sample size; no repeats on other days; time constraints may lead to rushed measurements. (b) Increase the number of samples; repeat on different days or seasons; use calibrated equipment; take means of repeats.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per limitation with explanation up to [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a method in which every individual or point has an equal chance of being selected, for example using random number tables to choose coordinates”?
items.answer: Random sampling
items.markingKey: Random sampling: a method in which every individual or point has an equal chance of being selected, for example using random number tables to choose coordinates. [1]

items.stem: Describe how random sampling with quadrats would be carried out in a field.
items.answer: Lay two tape measures at right angles along two edges to make a grid; use random number tables or a calculator to generate coordinates; place the quadrat at each coordinate; record species or percentage cover; repeat for at least 10 quadrats.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per step up to [4]

items.stem: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of systematic sampling.
items.answer: Advantages: quick and easy, gives even coverage, good for showing change along a gradient. Disadvantages: may miss or over-represent features that occur at regular intervals; not all points have an equal chance of selection.
items.markingKey: advantage [1]; disadvantage [1] [2]

items.stem: Students estimated a population of woodlice under logs near Mumbai. In the first sample they caught and marked 44. A day later they caught 25, of which 10 were marked. Suggest why the marks should be small and non-toxic.
items.answer: Large or bright marks could make animals easier for predators to see; toxic marks could kill them; both would reduce recaptures and overestimate the population.

items.stem: Students estimated a population of crabs on a rocky shore near Seoul. In the first sample they caught and marked 80. A day later they caught 29, of which 7 were marked. (a) State two assumptions made when using this method. (b) Suggest how the reliability of the estimate could be improved.
items.answer: (a) No migration, births or deaths between samples; marks do not affect survival or catchability; marked animals mix randomly with the population. (b) Repeat the capture several times and calculate a mean; increase the sample sizes; leave enough time for mixing.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: Students estimated a population of woodlice under logs near Toronto. In the first sample they caught and marked 56. A day later they caught 75, of which 5 were marked. (a) Use the Lincoln index N = (n₁ × n₂) ÷ m₂ to estimate the population. (b) State two assumptions made when using this method.
items.answer: (a) 840 (b) No migration, births or deaths between samples; marks do not affect survival or catchability; marked animals mix randomly with the population.

items.stem: A group is investigating whether trampling on a footpath affects plant species diversity in a park near Nairobi. The group has one day for data collection. The hypothesis is: “Species diversity increases with distance from the centre of the path.” (a) Explain how the data could be analysed to test the hypothesis. (b) Explain how the reliability of the results could be improved.
items.answer: (a) Plot a scatter graph (or bar chart for groups) and use Spearman’s rank correlation (or compare means) to test whether the relationship is significant at the 0.05 level, accepting or rejecting the null hypothesis. (b) Increase the number of samples; repeat on different days or seasons; use calibrated equipment; take means of repeats.
items.markingKey: (a) graph [1]; statistical test [1]; significance / null hypothesis [1] [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: Students want to know whether soil moisture affects the number of earthworms in a school field in Doha. The students have one day for data collection. items.answer: (a) Plot a scatter graph (or bar chart for groups) and use Spearman’s rank correlation (or compare means) to test whether the relationship is significant at the 0.05 level, accepting or rejecting the null hypothesis. (b) Conditions on one day may not be typical (weather, season); limited sample size; no repeats on other days; time constraints may lead to rushed measurements.
items.markingKey: (a) graph [1]; statistical test [1]; significance / null hypothesis [1] [3] (b) 1 mark per limitation with explanation up to [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Larger samples usually give more reliable results.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Larger samples reduce the effect of unusual individual results and are more representative of the population.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Students estimated a population of crabs on a rocky shore near Toronto. In the first sample they caught and marked 48. A day later they caught 38, of which 15 were marked. (a) State two assumptions made when using this method. (b) Suggest why the marks should be small and non-toxic. (c) Suggest how the reliability of the estimate could be improved.
items.answer: (a) No migration, births or deaths between samples; marks do not affect survival or catchability; marked animals mix randomly with the population. (b) Large or bright marks could make animals easier for predators to see; toxic marks could kill them; both would reduce recaptures and overestimate the population. (c) Repeat the capture several times and calculate a mean; increase the sample sizes; leave enough time for mixing.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a non-living physical or chemical feature of the environment, such as temperature, light, pH or soil moisture”?
items.answer: Abiotic factor
items.markingKey: Abiotic factor: a non-living physical or chemical feature of the environment, such as temperature, light, pH or soil moisture. [1]

items.stem: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of questionnaires compared with interviews.
items.answer: Questionnaires: quick, many respondents, easy to analyse, anonymous; but shallow answers, low response rates and misunderstood questions. Interviews: detailed, follow-up questions, explanation of views; but time-consuming, small samples, interviewer bias, harder to compare.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point, balance required, up to [4]

items.stem: Explain how to design a good questionnaire.
items.answer: Clear, simple, unambiguous questions; a mix of closed and some open questions; avoid leading questions; keep it short; logical order; pilot it first; include ethical statements on anonymity and consent.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [3]

items.stem: Soil samples were taken at three sites on a slope. Wet mass (g): A 67.6, B 70.6, C 55.6. Mass after oven-drying at 105 °C (g): A 49.5, B 61.5, C 46.6. (a) Suggest why site A has the highest moisture content. (b) Suggest one source of error in the method.
items.answer: (a) It may be lower on the slope where water collects, have more clay or organic matter, or be shaded so less evaporation. (b) Water lost from samples before weighing; samples not dried completely; different sample sizes or depths; balance precision.

items.stem: Soil samples were taken at three sites on a slope. Wet mass (g): A 76.4, B 48.2, C 60.5. Mass after oven-drying at 105 °C (g): A 49.5, B 36.5, C 46.6. (a) Calculate the percentage moisture content of each sample (as a percentage of wet mass). (b) Suggest why site A has the highest moisture content.
items.answer: (a) A 35.2%; B 24.3%; C 23.0% (b) It may be lower on the slope where water collects, have more clay or organic matter, or be shaded so less evaporation.
items.markingKey: (a) method [1]; all correct [1] [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: Samuel is investigating whether light intensity affects the height of plants growing under a woodland canopy. Samuel has one day for data collection. The hypothesis is: “Plant height increases with light intensity.” (a) Explain how the data could be analysed to test the hypothesis. (b) Explain how the reliability of the results could be improved.
items.answer: (a) Plot a scatter graph (or bar chart for groups) and use Spearman’s rank correlation (or compare means) to test whether the relationship is significant at the 0.05 level, accepting or rejecting the null hypothesis. (b) Increase the number of samples; repeat on different days or seasons; use calibrated equipment; take means of repeats.
items.markingKey: (a) graph [1]; statistical test [1]; significance / null hypothesis [1] [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: Soil samples were taken at three sites on a slope. Wet mass (g): A 54, B 48.7, C 59.6. Mass after oven-drying at 105 °C (g): A 33.9, B 37.7, C 34.5. What is the percentage moisture content of site A (calculated from the wet mass)?
Which term matches this definition: “a measure of biodiversity that takes into account both species richness and the evenness of their abundance”?
items.answer: Simpson's index of diversity
items.markingKey: Simpson's index of diversity: a measure of biodiversity that takes into account both species richness and the evenness of their abundance. [1]

items.stem: Explain why correlation does not prove causation.
items.answer: Two variables may be related by chance, or both may be affected by a third variable; an explanation must be supported by knowledge of processes.

items.stem: Explain why Simpson's index is more useful than species richness alone.
items.answer: It accounts for evenness as well as the number of species; a habitat dominated by one species has low diversity even if many species are present.

items.stem: Students counted organisms in a woodland floor: species A 7, species B 5, species C 23, species F 9. Simpson's index of diversity D = 1 − [Σn(n − 1) ÷ N(N − 1)]. Explain why the index takes account of evenness.
items.answer: The n(n − 1) terms give much more weight to abundant species, so a habitat dominated by one species has a low value even if many species are present.

items.stem: Students counted organisms in a woodland floor: species A 10, species B 15, species D 12, species E 14, species F 15. Simpson's index of diversity D = 1 − [Σn(n − 1) ÷ N(N − 1)]. (a) Explain why the index takes account of evenness. (b) Suggest one human activity that could reduce the diversity of this habitat.
items.answer: (a) The n(n − 1) terms give much more weight to abundant species, so a habitat dominated by one species has a low value even if many species are present. (b) Trampling, pollution, removal of vegetation, introduction of invasive species, use of herbicides or pesticides.

items.stem: Students counted organisms in a stream riffle: species A 24, species B 24, species C 11, species D 10, species E 3, species F 30. Simpson's index of diversity D = 1 − [Σn(n − 1) ÷ N(N − 1)]. (a) Calculate Simpson's index of diversity for the habitat. Show your working. (b) Suggest one human activity that could reduce the diversity of this habitat.
items.answer: (a) 0.788 (b) Trampling, pollution, removal of vegetation, introduction of invasive species, use of herbicides or pesticides.

items.stem: Leila is studying whether the concentration of nitrate in a river increases downstream of farmland. Leila has one day for data collection. The hypothesis is: “Nitrate concentration is higher downstream of farmland than upstream.” (a) Explain two limitations of a one-day study. (b) Explain how the reliability of the results could be improved.
items.answer: (a) Conditions on one day may not be typical (weather, season); limited sample size; no repeats on other days; time constraints may lead to rushed measurements. (b) Increase the number of samples; repeat on different days or seasons; use calibrated equipment; take means of repeats.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per limitation with explanation up to [2] (b) [2]

items.answer: (a) Plot a scatter graph (or bar chart for groups) and use Spearman’s rank correlation (or compare means) to test whether the relationship is significant at the 0.05 level, accepting or rejecting the null hypothesis. items.markingKey: (a) graph [1]; statistical test [1]; significance / null hypothesis [1] [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “A Spearman's rank value of +1 shows a perfect positive correlation between the ranks.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Every pair of ranks is the same.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Students recorded distance from the city centre (km) and PM2.5 concentration (μg/m³) at 8 sites: site 1: 14, 94; site 2: 61, 100; site 3: 63, 95.2; site 4: 127, 10; site 5: 130, 59.4; site 6: 148, 82.7; site 7: 171, 35.1; site 8: 187, 39.6. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)). The critical value for n = 8 at the 0.05 significance level is 0.738. (a) State a null hypothesis for this investigation. (b) Describe the direction and strength of the relationship. (c) Explain why a scatter graph should also be drawn.
items.answer: (a) There is no relationship between distance from the city centre and PM2.5 concentration. (b) Negative and moderate (rs = −0.64). (c) It shows the pattern visually, including anomalies and whether the relationship is linear or curved.

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the extent to which a method gives consistent results when it is repeated”?
items.answer: Reliability
items.markingKey: Reliability: the extent to which a method gives consistent results when it is repeated. [1]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the extent to which a method gives consistent results when it is repeated”?
items.answer: Reliability
items.markingKey: Reliability: the extent to which a method gives consistent results when it is repeated. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between accuracy and precision.
items.answer: Accuracy is how close a result is to the true value; precision is how close repeated readings are to each other. Results can be precise but inaccurate if there is a systematic error.
items.markingKey: accuracy [1]; precision [1] [2]

items.stem: Three repeat readings of soil pH were taken at one site: 6, 6.9, 6.1. Suggest two possible causes of the anomalous reading.
items.answer: Error in reading or recording the instrument; a change in conditions (e.g. a gust of wind, cloud, obstruction in the stream); equipment fault or not calibrated; measuring at a different point.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A researcher is investigating whether noise from traffic affects the number of bird species heard in urban parks in Istanbul. The researcher chose sites where it was easy to reach, took single readings and did not record the weather. (a) Explain whether the conclusions would be valid. (b) Suggest how secondary data could support the findings.
items.answer: (a) Conclusions are of limited validity because other variables (time of day, season, weather, duration of each count, the same observer) may not have been controlled and the sample may not be representative; a correlation would not prove that traffic noise level (dB) causes changes in number of bird species recorded in 10 minutes. (b) Compare with published studies, government monitoring data or long-term records for the same area to see if the pattern is consistent.

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a statement that there is no relationship or difference between the variables being studied”?
items.answer: Null hypothesis
items.markingKey: Null hypothesis: a statement that there is no relationship or difference between the variables being studied. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between primary and secondary data and give one advantage of each.
items.answer: Primary data is collected by the investigator (e.g. quadrat counts) and is specific to the aim; secondary data is collected by others (e.g. census, Met Office records) and may cover larger areas or longer periods.
items.markingKey: definitions [1]; advantages [1] [2]

items.stem: Students in Cape Town want to find out whether distance from a road affects the abundance of lichens on tree trunks. (a) Write a hypothesis for this investigation. (b) Write a null hypothesis.
items.answer: (a) Lichen cover increases with distance from the road. (b) There is no relationship between distance from the road and lichen cover.
items.markingKey: (a) testable, names both variables [1] (b) [1]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “taking samples at regular intervals, for example every 5 m along a transect or every 10th person”?
items.answer: Systematic sampling
items.markingKey: Systematic sampling: taking samples at regular intervals, for example every 5 m along a transect or every 10th person. [1]

items.stem: Explain when stratified sampling should be used.
items.answer: When the area or population contains distinct sub-groups (e.g. different habitats, land uses or age groups) of different sizes, so that each is represented in proportion.

items.stem: Yusuf placed 10 1 m × 1 m quadrats at random in a 400 m² field and counted buttercups in each: 12, 13, 4, 14, 3, 1, 12, 4, 2, 7. (a) Calculate the mean number per quadrat. (b) Explain why random sampling was used.
items.answer: (a) 7.2 (b) To avoid bias in choosing where to place quadrats, so the sample is representative of the field.

items.stem: Amara placed 10 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrats at random in a 1 200 m² field and counted buttercups in each: 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 10, 13, 13, 9, 2. (a) Calculate the population density per m². (b) Estimate the total population in the field. (c) Explain why random sampling was used.
items.answer: (a) 35.2 per m² (b) 42 240 (c) To avoid bias in choosing where to place quadrats, so the sample is representative of the field.

items.stem: Students want to know whether soil moisture affects the number of earthworms in a school field in Kathmandu. The students used a different piece of equipment at the last two sites after the first one broke, and collected data on two different days. (a) Evaluate the reliability of the method. (b) Suggest how secondary data could support the findings.
items.answer: (a) Changing equipment may introduce a systematic difference between sites; conditions differed between the two days, so differences may not be caused by the independent variable; results are not directly comparable. (b) Compare with published studies, government monitoring data or long-term records for the same area to see if the pattern is consistent.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per developed point up to [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “abiotic factor”?
options: A set of written questions used to collect information from a sample of people.
A living feature of the environment that affects organisms, such as predation, competition or disease.
A question with a fixed set of possible answers, such as yes/no or a rating scale.
A non-living physical or chemical feature of the environment, such as temperature, light, pH or soil moisture.
items.answer: A non-living physical or chemical feature of the environment, such as temperature, light, pH or soil moisture.
items.markingKey: Abiotic factor: a non-living physical or chemical feature of the environment, such as temperature, light, pH or soil moisture. [1]

items.stem: Describe how to measure the velocity of a stream.
items.answer: Measure a set distance (e.g. 10 m); drop a float upstream; time how long it takes to travel the distance; repeat three times and calculate mean time; velocity = distance ÷ time (or use a flow meter).
items.markingKey: 1 mark per step up to [3]

items.stem: Students in Dubai designed a questionnaire about attitudes to a new national park. They asked 40 people in the town centre on a weekday morning; 11 supported the proposal. Suggest how the sampling could be improved.
items.answer: Stratified sampling by age or area; survey at different times and days and in different places; a larger sample.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “A correlation coefficient of 0.4 is always significant.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Significance depends on the number of pairs; with small samples a much higher value is needed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Describe how to test a relationship using Spearman's rank.
items.answer: State null hypothesis; rank each variable; find the difference d for each pair and square it; calculate rs = 1 − 6Σd²/(n(n² − 1)); compare with the critical value for n at 0.05; accept or reject the null hypothesis.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per step up to [4]

items.stem: Students recorded light intensity (lux) and plant height (cm) at 8 sites: site 1: 22, 29.9; site 2: 39, 20.7; site 3: 62, 10; site 4: 73, 51.8; site 5: 131, 81.5; site 6: 165, 95.3; site 7: 168, 100; site 8: 199, 99.1. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)). The critical value for n = 8 at the 0.05 significance level is 0.738. (a) State a null hypothesis for this investigation. (b) Describe the direction and strength of the relationship.
items.answer: (a) There is no relationship between light intensity and plant height. (b) Positive and strong (rs = 0.88).

items.stem: Explain how to estimate percentage cover using a quadrat divided into 100 small squares.
items.answer: Count the number of small squares that are more than half covered by the species; each square is 1%, so the count gives the percentage cover.

items.stem: A village near Singapore has 8 000 people aged 16-29, 5 000 aged 30-59 and 9 000 aged 60 and over. Students will ask 80 people about their views on a proposed wind farm, using stratified sampling. Describe how the samples would be chosen within each group.
items.answer: Within each age group, choose people randomly (e.g. every nth house or random numbers from the electoral roll) and ask their age before the survey.

items.answer: (a) 206; the estimate is very sensitive to the number recaptured, so small errors matter. (b) Repeat the capture several times and calculate a mean; increase the sample sizes; leave enough time for mixing.

items.stem: Students want to know whether soil moisture affects the number of earthworms in a school field in Bogotá. The students have one day for data collection. The hypothesis is: “The number of earthworms increases as soil moisture increases.” (a) Explain two limitations of a one-day study. (b) Explain how the reliability of the results could be improved.
items.answer: (a) Conditions on one day may not be typical (weather, season); limited sample size; no repeats on other days; time constraints may lead to rushed measurements. (b) Increase the number of samples; repeat on different days or seasons; use calibrated equipment; take means of repeats.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per limitation with explanation up to [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “biotic factor”?
options: A question that allows the respondent to answer freely in their own words.
A question with a fixed set of possible answers, such as yes/no or a rating scale.
A set of written questions used to collect information from a sample of people.
A living feature of the environment that affects organisms, such as predation, competition or disease.
items.answer: A living feature of the environment that affects organisms, such as predation, competition or disease.
items.markingKey: Biotic factor: a living feature of the environment that affects organisms, such as predation, competition or disease. [1]

items.stem: Describe how wind speed could be measured accurately during fieldwork in Cairo.
items.answer: Use an anemometer; hold at a set height, facing into the wind, for a set time; take repeat readings at each site and calculate a mean.
items.markingKey: equipment [1]; technique for accuracy [1]; repeats / mean [1] [3]

items.stem: Soil samples were taken at three sites on a slope. Wet mass (g): A 70.4, B 52.9, C 47.5. Mass after oven-drying at 105 °C (g): A 62, B 41.5, C 41.1. (a) Explain why the samples were dried to constant mass. (b) Suggest one source of error in the method.
items.answer: (a) To make sure all the water had evaporated, so the mass lost is the total water content. (b) Water lost from samples before weighing; samples not dried completely; different sample sizes or depths; balance precision.

items.stem: A news article states: “A higher Simpson’s index means the habitat is more stable and diverse.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Higher diversity usually means more complex food webs and greater resilience to change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why Simpson's index is more useful than species richness alone. (b) A news article states: “A higher Simpson’s index means the habitat is more stable and diverse.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) It accounts for evenness as well as the number of species; a habitat dominated by one species has low diversity even if many species are present. (b) Correct. Higher diversity usually means more complex food webs and greater resilience to change.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Students counted organisms in a woodland floor: species B 3, species C 14, species D 23, species F 18. Simpson's index of diversity D = 1 − [Σn(n − 1) ÷ N(N − 1)]. Explain why the index takes account of evenness.
items.answer: The n(n − 1) terms give much more weight to abundant species, so a habitat dominated by one species has a low value even if many species are present.

items.stem: Students recorded altitude (m) and air temperature (°C) at 10 sites: site 1: 23, 77.4; site 2: 74, 35.6; site 3: 110, 55.3; site 4: 132, 100; site 5: 151, 33.5; site 6: 154, 38.4; site 7: 164, 16.9; site 8: 169, 46.3; site 9: 173, 38.8; site 10: 179, 10. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)). The critical value for n = 10 at the 0.05 significance level is 0.648. (a) State a null hypothesis for this investigation. (b) Describe the direction and strength of the relationship. (c) Explain why a scatter graph should also be drawn.
items.answer: (a) There is no relationship between altitude and air temperature. (b) Negative and moderate (rs = −0.52). (c) It shows the pattern visually, including anomalies and whether the relationship is linear or curved.

items.stem: A group is investigating whether trampling on a footpath affects plant species diversity in a park near Bogotá. The group has one day for data collection. The hypothesis is: “Species diversity increases with distance from the centre of the path.” (a) Explain two limitations of a one-day study. (b) Explain how the reliability of the results could be improved.
items.answer: (a) Conditions on one day may not be typical (weather, season); limited sample size; no repeats on other days; time constraints may lead to rushed measurements. (b) Increase the number of samples; repeat on different days or seasons; use calibrated equipment; take means of repeats.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per limitation with explanation up to [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Anomalous results should be discussed in an evaluation.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Explaining possible causes of anomalies shows understanding of the method’s limitations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Three repeat readings of noise level were taken at one site: 75 dB, 59 dB, 57 dB. Calculate the percentage difference between the mean including the anomaly and the mean excluding it.

Students want to know whether soil moisture affects the number of earthworms in a school field in Auckland. The students sampled only 5 sites, all on one afternoon, and took one reading at each site. (a) Suggest improvements to the method and explain how each would improve the investigation. (b) Suggest how secondary data could support the findings.
items.answer: (a) Increase the number of sites (e.g. 10-15) across the full range of soil moisture (%); take three repeats and calculate means; random or systematic site selection to avoid bias; use the same calibrated equipment; collect all data under similar conditions. (b) Compare with published studies, government monitoring data or long-term records for the same area to see if the pattern is consistent.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per improvement with explanation up to [4] (b) [1]
